name: Lexical Coverage Analysis
description: Measures text comprehension coverage based on high-frequency word lists — AI text shows different coverage profiles.
algorithm: Frequency Band Coverage and Vocabulary Profiling
mechanism:
This method applies Lexical Coverage Analysis for AI-generated content detection:

1. **Frequency Band Profiling**: The method classifies every word token in the text into frequency bands using Nation's (2006) BNC/COCA word family lists: K1 (1st 1000 most frequent families), K2 (2nd 1000), K3 (3rd 1000), through K20+ (beyond 20,000). For each band, the method computes the proportion of text tokens falling within it. Human text shows a characteristic coverage curve: K1 covers 70–80% of tokens, K1+K2 covers 82–90%, and each subsequent band adds progressively less. AI text shows a compressed coverage curve: K1 covers 78–88% (higher than human), K1+K2 covers 88–95%, with fewer tokens in bands K5 and beyond. This reflects AI's tendency to over-rely on common vocabulary. The method computes the coverage curve shape using the Gini coefficient of frequency band distribution: human Gini 0.70–0.80; AI Gini 0.82–0.92 (more concentrated).

2. **Off-List and Low-Frequency Word Analysis**: Words not found in the top 20,000 families (off-list words) are particularly diagnostic. These include domain-specific terminology, proper nouns, neologisms, informal language, and rare words. Human text contains 3–8% off-list tokens; AI text contains 1–4%. The method further analyzes off-list word types: (a) technical terms — domain-specific vocabulary indicating expertise, (b) proper nouns — named entities suggesting specific knowledge, (c) colloquial/slang — informal language indicating register awareness, (d) rare literary words — low-frequency but established words. Human off-list vocabulary distributes across all 4 types; AI off-list vocabulary concentrates on technical terms with little colloquial or literary range.

3. **Vocabulary Sophistication Index**: Beyond frequency, the method computes vocabulary sophistication using the P_Lex measure (Meara & Bell, 2001) — the proportion of 'difficult' words (beyond K2) in the text's lexical profile. Human text shows P_Lex values calibrated to register: academic 0.15–0.25, journalism 0.08–0.15, conversation 0.03–0.08. AI text shows less register calibration — producing P_Lex of 0.08–0.14 regardless of target register, undershoot for academic and overshoot for conversational. The method also computes the Academic Word List (AWL, Coxhead 2000) coverage: human academic text uses 8–12% AWL tokens; AI text uses 10–16% (over-representing academic vocabulary even in non-academic contexts).

4. **Lexical Diversity by Frequency Band**: The method measures how diversely each frequency band is used — not just how many tokens fall in K3, but how many different word types from K3 appear. This is computed as the type-token ratio (TTR) within each band. Human text shows decreasing TTR across bands (0.4–0.7 in K1, 0.7–0.9 in K5+) — using common words repetitively but rare words more uniquely. AI text shows flatter TTR across bands (0.3–0.5 in K1, 0.5–0.7 in K5+) — using both common and rare words with similar repetitiveness. The method computes TTR-band gradient: human gradient 0.05–0.10 per band; AI gradient 0.01–0.04 per band.
parameters:
Frequency bands: K1 through K20+ (Nation's BNC/COCA lists)
K1 coverage human: 70–80%
K1 coverage AI: 78–88%
Gini coefficient human: 0.70–0.80
Gini coefficient AI: 0.82–0.92
Off-list tokens human: 3–8%
Off-list tokens AI: 1–4%
P_Lex academic human: 0.15–0.25
P_Lex AI (all registers): 0.08–0.14
AWL coverage human academic: 8–12%
AWL coverage AI: 10–16%
Minimum text length: 200 words
accuracy: 76–85% accuracy detecting AI-generated text via lexical coverage analysis. Frequency band Gini coefficient achieves AUC of 0.81. Off-list word analysis adds 3–4% improvement. Vocabulary sophistication provides F1-score of 0.79. Performance best for general prose; lower for highly technical text where both human and AI use similar vocabulary.
source: Nation, I. S. P. (2006). How large a vocabulary is needed for reading and listening? Canadian Modern Language Review, 63(1), 59–82.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated text through vocabulary frequency profile analysis. Assessing L2 writing proficiency through coverage patterns. Identifying AI-written educational materials through compressed vocabulary. Evaluating readability and vocabulary appropriateness in publishing.
strengths:
• Well-established vocabulary research foundation (Nation, Coxhead)
• Frequency band analysis is computationally efficient
• Register sensitivity catches AI's failure to adapt vocabulary
• Off-list analysis targets AI's avoidance of rare/specialized words
• Complementary to lexical diversity and sophistication methods
limitations:
• Frequency lists are corpus-dependent and may not cover all domains
• L2 writers show similar compressed coverage profiles
• Technical text naturally has high off-list rates regardless of source
• Very short texts may not have stable frequency distributions
• AI fine-tuned on specific registers may show appropriate coverage

references.title: Nation, I. S. P. — How large a vocabulary is needed for reading and listening? (Canadian Modern Language Review 2006)
Coxhead, A. — A New Academic Word List (TESOL Quarterly 2000)
Meara, P. & Bell, H. — P_Lex: A Simple and Effective Way of Describing the Lexical Characteristics of Short L2 Texts (Prospect 2001)
